levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
You are an incident responder tasked with investigating a potential compromise involving the Sofacy group's Fysbis backdoor on a Linux-based network. The Fysbis malware is known to be a modular Linux trojan/backdoor that implements plug-in and controller modules as distinct classes. It includes both 32-bit and 64-bit versions of ELF binaries and can install itself with or without root privileges.

Your goal is to identify and investigate the suspicious activity, determine the extent of the compromise, and take appropriate containment measures.

levels.title: Suspicious Service Discovery
levels.content: While monitoring the network, you noticed unusual outbound connections from the target host. Investigate the target host to identify any unauthorized or suspicious services running on the system. The flag is the name of the suspicious service.
levels.solution:
To identify suspicious services, you can use the following commands:

1. List all running services:
   `systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running`

2. Check for any unfamiliar or suspicious services.

3. Investigate the service files and configurations for any signs of tampering.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the list of running services and look for any that seem out of place or unfamiliar.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Examine the systemd service files and timers to find any related to the suspicious service.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The suspicious service is likely to have an unusual name or configuration. Look for services that do not match standard system services.

levels.title: Persistence Discovery
levels.content: You have identified a suspicious service running on the target host. Determine how this service is automatically started after a system reboot. The flag is the path to the systemd timer file.
levels.solution:
To identify persistence mechanisms, you can use the following commands:

1. List all systemd service files:
   `ls /etc/systemd/system/`

2. Check the contents of the service files for any suspicious configurations.

3. Investigate the systemd timers for any related to the suspicious service.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Examine the systemd service files and timers to find any related to the suspicious service.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Look for any unusual or unexpected configurations in the service files.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The persistence mechanism is likely to be a systemd timer file. Look for files with a .timer extension.

levels.title: C2 Communication Discovery (Port)
levels.content: The suspicious service appears to be communicating with an external command-and-control (C2) server. Determine which network port is used for this communication. The flag is the network port used for C2 communication.
levels.solution:
To identify the network port used for C2 communication, you can use the following commands:

1. List all network connections:
   `ss -tulnp`

2. Check for any unusual or unexpected network connections.

3. Investigate the network traffic for any signs of C2 communication.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the network connections and listen ports to identify any unusual or unexpected network activity.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Look for any unusual or unexpected network connections in the output of the `ss -tulnp` command.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The C2 communication is likely to be on a standard port. Look for ports that are commonly used for web traffic.
